main_issue: The three cases consistently indicate general-purpose object deserialization on attacker-reachable or insufficiently trusted input. The main case-specific uncertainty is the exact trust boundary and deserializer configuration for the Seata and Emissary anchors, rather than a conflicting vulnerability mechanism.
evidence_notes: CVE-2025-47771 has direct evidence: SparseMatrix.read creates ObjectInputStream and invokes readObject on the supplied InputStream without prior type filtering or validation; its writer uses writeObject(this), confirming native Java object serialization.

CVE-2021-32634 is labeled CWE-502 and its PayloadUtil/WorkBundle anchors are consistent with Java payload deserialization, but the payload entrypoint, attacker control, and any existing ObjectInputFilter or equivalent guard are not shown in the supplied evidence.

CVE-2025-32897 anchors CustomDeserializer plus Raft snapshot and sync serializers, which is consistent with unsafe cluster-message or snapshot deserialization; evidence should confirm whether peers, snapshots, or replication inputs can be attacker-controlled and whether serializer type restrictions existed before the fix.

The guideline names the relevant source-to-sink shape, missing type/side-effect constraint, and practical remediation options. Its requirement to confirm the guard on the same path appropriately avoids reporting benign internal-only serialization.
